status: drafted via direct reading of the real Geneva Bible 1560 extracted verse text (Assets/Resources/Verses/Geneva/lamentations_25.json); cross-checked against the existing KJV Lamentations Character Index for pattern consistency only, not copied blindly. Not yet adversarially fact-checked by a second pass.
notes:
Lamentations in the Geneva 1560 translation is, like the KJV, five poems of funeral lament over Jerusalem's fall to Babylon: chapters 1, 2, 4, and 5 are 22-verse acrostics (one stanza per Hebrew letter, invisible in English but structurally present via the verse-per-letter count), chapter 3 is a 66-verse triple acrostic and the book's theological center, containing 3:22-23 ("great is thy faithfulnesse"). Total verse count read directly from the source file: 22+22+66+22+22 = 154, exactly matching the book's stated scope — confirming the Geneva text has NO structural divergence from the standard canon for this book (unlike, e.g., the Ethiopian Bible's genuinely different 9-chapter Ezra).

METHODOLOGY DEVIATION FLAGGED (same as the KJV index for this book, independently re-confirmed by reading the real Geneva text): the book names zero individual persons anywhere — not the poet, not the besieging king, not "the Anoynted of the Lord" taken in 4:20, not "the man" of 3:1. All five scribe tiers are therefore role:"law" (theme/content-type), not person-type. There are consequently no submanagers, no genealogy entries, and no ageEvents anywhere in this index — a deliberate, book-driven absence. Every scribeTiers[].managerId resolves 1:1 to a real characters[].id; every characters[].deliveredBy is null (not a dangling reference) since there is no individual author or speaker named in the text to attribute delivery to — the anonymous-authorship/traditional-Jeremiah-attribution hedge is folded into each tier's purpose text instead.

NAMING-COLLISION CHECK: not applicable — no proper personal name appears anywhere in this book to collide with any other figure in this or any other translation's index.

REAL TRANSLATION-LEVEL WORDING DIFFERENCES FOUND vs. the existing KJV index (verified by direct comparison of the actual extracted texts, flagged rather than silently normalized, per the project's scripture-accuracy rule): Lamentations 4:20 — Geneva reads "taken in their nets," where the KJV reads "taken in their pits" (same event — the capture of "the Anoynted/anointed of the Lord," likely King Zedekiah per 2 Kings 25:5-7, still not named in-text in either translation — but a genuinely different word choice, not an extraction artifact). Lamentations 5:22, the book's actual final verse — Geneva reads "But thou hast vtterly reiected vs: thou art exceedingly angry against vs," where the KJV reads "thou art very sore displeased against us" — again a real, distinct wording choice preserved as-is, not corrected toward the more familiar KJV phrasing.

AUTHORSHIP HEDGE (applies to all 5 tiers): the Geneva text, like the Hebrew original, never names an author. Tradition (a Septuagint/Vulgate-derived heading, not the underlying Hebrew text itself) ascribes the book to Jeremiah; this is noted as tradition only, never asserted as textual fact.

This is a small, fully self-contained 5-tier index reflecting the book's genuine scope in this translation — not an attempt to force a larger person/manager roster onto a book that structurally doesn't contain one, in Geneva any more than in KJV.

New Every Morning (Great Is Thy Faithfulnesse)

characters.name: The Widow City — Jerusalem's Desolation (Lamentations 1, Geneva)
characters.purpose: Personifies Jerusalem as a great city fallen to the status of a bereaved widow — 'full of people' now 'solitarie,' weeping continually in the night with none to comfort her, all her former lovers/friends turned unfaithful — while the chapter itself concedes late on that the judgment is deserved: 'The Lord is righteous: for I haue rebelled against his commandement' (1:18). No individual person or author is named anywhere in this chapter of the Geneva text; the lament is spoken in and through the personified city herself.

verses.note: "Howe doeth the citie remaine solitarie that was full of people? she is as a widowe... She weepeth continually in the night, and her teares runne downe by her cheekes: among all her louers, she hath none to comfort her."
"Haue ye no regarde, all yee that passe by this way? behold, and see, if there be any sorowe like vnto my sorowe" — the chapter's central appeal to onlookers.
"The Lord is righteous: for I haue rebelled against his commandement" — the lament's own admission that the disaster is deserved, not arbitrary.

funFacts: Chapter 1 is a 22-verse acrostic in the underlying Hebrew (one verse per Hebrew letter), a structural feature invisible in this English translation but reflected in the exact 22-verse count.
Jerusalem/Zion is addressed throughout as a specific grieving woman ('she'/'her'), not described merely as an abstract city.

characters.name: The Darkened Cloud — The Lord's Day of Wrath (Lamentations 2, Geneva)
characters.scribeTier: The Darkened Cloud (The Lord's Day of Wrath)
characters.purpose: Names the Lord himself as the direct agent of Jerusalem's ruin — 'The Lord was as an enemie: he hath deuoured Israel' (2:5) — cataloguing the destroyed sanctuary, forgotten feasts and Sabbaths, fallen king and priest, and indicting the nation's own prophets for having 'looked out vayne, and foolish things' instead of exposing the people's iniquity and warning them (2:14). No individual is named anywhere in the chapter.

verses.note: "How hath the Lord darkened the daughter of Zion in his wrath!... and remembred not his footestoole in the day of his wrath!"
"The Lord was as an enemie: he hath deuoured Israel, and consumed all his palaces" — the chapter's central, startling reversal, God described in the language normally used for Israel's foes.
"Mine eyes doe saile with teares: my bowels swell... because the children and sucklings swoone in the streetes of the citie."

"Thy Prophets haue looked out vayne, and foolish things for thee, and they haue not discouered thine iniquitie, to turne away thy captiuitie, but haue looked out for thee false prophesies, and causes of banishment." — the nation's own prophets blamed for failing to warn of judgment.

funFacts: Chapter 2 is also a 22-verse acrostic in the underlying Hebrew, like chapters 1, 4, and 5.

characters.name: New Every Morning — "Great Is Thy Faithfulnesse" (Lamentations 3, Geneva)
characters.scribeTier: New Every Morning (Great Is Thy Faithfulnesse)
characters.purpose: The book's structural and theological center: an unnamed sufferer, 'the man, that hath seene affliction in the rod of his indignation' (3:1), descends into personal darkness under God's discipline, then turns at the chapter's midpoint to the book's most famous affirmation of hope, 'his compassions faile not... great is thy faithfulnesse' (3:22-23), before returning later in the same chapter to lament and a plea for the Lord to judge his oppressors. The Geneva text, like the Hebrew, never states who 'the man' is.

verses.note: "I am the man, that hath seene affliction in the rod of his indignation." — opens the chapter's first-person lament.

"It is the Lordes mercies that wee are not consumed, because his compassions faile not. They are renued euery morning: great is thy faithfulnesse." — the book's most quoted lines, at the exact center of its longest chapter.
"The Lord is good vnto them, that trust in him, and to the soule that seeketh him... It is good both to trust, and to waite for the saluation of the Lord."

"I called vpon thy Name, O Lord, out of the lowe dungeon. Thou hast heard my voyce: stoppe not thine eare from my sigh and from my cry." — the sufferer testifies God has already heard him, mid-lament.

funFacts: Chapter 3 is a triple acrostic in the underlying Hebrew — 66 verses in which each set of three consecutive verses shares an opening letter, cycling through all 22 letters — making it both the longest chapter in the book and its most tightly structured.

The hope of 3:22-23 is bracketed by continued lament within the same chapter (verses 1-20 before it, renewed complaint later on) — the Geneva text, like every other translation of this book, does not resolve into unbroken comfort even here.

characters.name: The Dimmed Golde — Siege and Famine (Lamentations 4, Geneva)
characters.purpose: Contrasts Zion's former glory — her 'noble men... coparable to fine golde' (4:1-2) — with the horrors of the siege's famine, including compassionate mothers reduced to boiling their own children for meat (4:10), lays blame on corrupt priests and prophets who 'shed the blood of the iust' (4:13), and mourns the capture of 'the Anoynted of the Lord' (4:20) before closing with a taunt-oracle against Edom (4:21-22). No individual is named by proper name anywhere in the chapter.

verses.note: "How is the golde become so dimme?... The noble men of Zion coparable to fine golde, howe are they esteemed as earthen pitchers, euen the worke of the handes of the potter!" — former splendor contrasted with present ruin.
"The hands of the pitifull women haue sodden their owne children, which were their meate in the destruction of the daughter of my people." — the siege's famine at its most extreme.
"For the sinnes of her Prophets, and the iniquities of her Priests, that haue shed the blood of the iust in the middes of her."

"The breath of our nostrels, the Anoynted of the Lord was taken in their nets, of whome we sayde, Vnder his shadowe we shalbe preserued aliue among the heathen." NOTE: Geneva reads 'taken in their nets' where the existing KJV index reads 'taken in their pits' — a real, verified wording difference between the two translations, not an extraction error. Widely connected by later interpreters to King Zedekiah's capture (compare 2 Kings 25:5-7, a separate passage), but no individual is named in this verse itself — treat any such identification as inference, not textual fact.

"Reioyce and be glad, O daughter Edom, that dwellest in the lande of Vz, the cuppe also shall passe through vnto thee: thou shalt be drunken and vomit." — a taunt-oracle warning Edom that judgment will reach her too.

funFacts: Chapter 4 is another 22-verse acrostic in the underlying Hebrew, with shorter (two-line) verses than chapters 1-2's three-line verses.
Edom (4:21-22) is a neighboring nation descended from Esau, not an individual person — a named group/place referenced in the text, not a character entry of its own.
4:20's 'taken in their nets' (Geneva) vs. the KJV's 'taken in their pits' is a genuine, directly-verified translation wording difference worth noting for anyone comparing the two indexes.

characters.name: Remember, O Lord — Prayer for Restoration (Lamentations 5, Geneva)
characters.purpose: A closing communal prayer spoken in the corporate voice of 'we'/'vs,' asking the Lord to 'remember' and 'behold' the nation's reproach — lost inheritance, fatherless children, enslaved elders, hunger, and violated women — and ending with a plea for restoration ('Turne thou vs vnto thee, O Lord,' 5:21) that the chapter deliberately leaves unresolved rather than triumphantly answered ('thou hast vtterly reiected vs: thou art exceedingly angry against vs,' 5:22).

verses.note: "Remember, O Lord, what is come vpon vs: consider, and behold our reproche." — opens the closing prayer.
"Our fathers haue sinned, and are not, and we haue borne their iniquities." — the generation praying acknowledges bearing consequences beyond their own acts.
"They defiled the women in Zion, and the maydes in the cities of Iudah." — among the atrocities catalogued in the prayer.
"Turne thou vs vnto thee, O Lord, and we shalbe turned: renue our dayes as of olde." — the book's climactic plea for restoration.

"But thou hast vtterly reiected vs: thou art exceedingly angry against vs." — the book's actual final verse in Geneva, deliberately unresolved. NOTE: reads 'thou art exceedingly angry against vs' where the existing KJV index reads 'thou art very sore displeased against us' — a real, verified wording difference between the two translations.

funFacts: Chapter 5 has 22 verses like chapters 1, 2, and 4, but is NOT itself an acrostic in the underlying Hebrew — the only one of the five poems to abandon the alphabetic structure, which many readers connect to its closing, unresolved tone.
Geneva's final verse wording ('exceedingly angry') is noticeably harsher in tone than the KJV's ('very sore displeased') — worth flagging for anyone comparing translations side by side.

genealogyLists.note: Lamentations (Geneva) contains no genealogies and no bulk name lists of any kind, confirmed by direct reading of the full extracted text. Every chapter is poetic lament addressed corporately to 'Zion'/'the daughter of my people'/'we, vs' — the text names no individual person anywhere in the book: not the poet, not the besieging king, not 'the Anoynted of the Lord' taken in 4:20, and not 'the man' who speaks in 3:1. This is a genuine structural feature of the book in this translation too, not an omission on this pass — there is nothing to place in a genealogy or bulk-name list for this entry.
